How Decision Lab Was Built

PLAIN-ENGLISH METHODS · 4 PAGES

How real school data, research, simulation, intervention logic, and future program learning fit together.

Read PDF ↗ Download Word ↓

A Dashboard Tells You What Happened. Decision Lab Lets You Rehearse What Happens Next.

A school-level simulation system for decisions that are too important to make by straight-line projection alone.

Every administrator knows the uncomfortable part of school improvement: by the time the data proves a strategy worked—or did not—the year is already moving on. Decision Lab is designed for the moment before that happens.

A forecast extends the current line. That is useful when the world behaves politely. Schools rarely do. Attendance changes academic pressure. Academic pressure affects engagement. Engagement affects participation. Two interventions may reach the same students. Staff capacity can turn a promising plan into an impossible one. Over time, the variables begin to bump into one another—and every collision can change what happens next.

Simulation is built for that messiness. Instead of asking only “Where are we headed?”, Decision Lab asks “What might happen if we change the conditions?” Modern computing and AI make it practical to evaluate many interacting conditions at once—in an explainable form.

ForecastWhere are we headed?Extends current conditions into a likely future.
SimulationWhat if we change the conditions?Tests goals, reach, overlap, staffing limits, cross-goal effects and alternative scenarios before committing resources.
A forecast gives you one likely road. A simulation lets you test the turns before you take them.
Your campus. Your goals. Your constraints. A modeled plan. The purpose is not certainty. It is a better-informed choice.

Your School Is Not a Demo Variable.

The model begins with official public data about the selected campus—not a generic “average high school.”

The California demonstration includes baseline records for 1,267 public high schools. Choose the county, district and school, and Decision Lab loads available campus measures with appropriate district, county and California comparisons. The simulation should start from the school administrators actually lead.

Official public school data establishes the baseline. Research-quality longitudinal evidence helps describe relationships that aggregate reports cannot show by themselves. Decision Lab then tests what could happen next.

California Department of Education · DataQuest
California School Dashboard

DERIVEDCalculations made from public information and clearly labeled.

Real school first. Research second. Simulation third. No sleight of hand.
Decision Lab projections are modeled planning estimates—not California Department of Education or NCES forecasts.

The Numbers Tell You What. The Relationships Help Explain Why.

Decision Lab combines school baselines, longitudinal research, and a growing intervention-response learning loop.

Public school data is excellent at telling administrators what happened. It is much weaker at showing the joint relationships underneath the result. Decision Lab therefore adds research-quality longitudinal evidence from the U.S. Department of Education’s National Center for Education Statistics, including studies that follow real students across time.

Then the system can begin to learn from the intervention itself. Peer-to-Peer Planner, Homework Habit and the Citizenship Score can generate behavioral and intervention-response training data ordinary school databases usually do not capture—planning consistency, homework routines, peer participation, recognition, engagement, intervention exposure and the response that follows.

Baseline → intervention → response → outcome → a better next simulation.
“Training data” is used here in the practical AI sense: signals that can help recalibrate the model as validated local evidence accumulates.
Development leadership. Decision Lab is being developed under the leadership of Craig Moncreiff, founder of Homework Habit and the Total Campus Initiative. Moncreiff previously served as Publisher of Software at John Wiley & Sons (NYSE: WLY)—a $1.5 billion publisher whose history includes Edgar Allan Poe and whose modern catalog includes the For Dummies franchise. The technology can be complex. The administrator-facing product cannot be.

Evidence & Methods

Research & Official Data Foundation

Decision Lab begins with two different kinds of evidence: official information about the school you actually lead, and national longitudinal research that helps describe how student conditions relate over time. The two principal public authorities are the California Department of Education and the U.S. Department of Education's National Center for Education Statistics. The simulation layer is kept separate from both.

NCES
OFFICIAL SOURCE

Model Research · U.S. Department of Education

The current research foundation includes the NCES Education Longitudinal Study of 2002 (ELS:2002), a nationally representative longitudinal high-school study used in model development and calibration. It helps Decision Lab represent relationships among student conditions that a school-level dashboard cannot show by itself.

U.S. Department of Education›Institute of Education Sciences›NCES›ELS:2002
CA
OFFICIAL SOURCE

Your School Data · California Department of Education

School identity and available baseline and benchmark values are drawn from California Department of Education DataQuest and official downloadable public data files. The selected school's real public baseline is the starting point for the scenario.

CA
OFFICIAL CDE ACCOUNTABILITY SYSTEM
California School Dashboard

The Dashboard is California's public accountability and continuous-improvement system. It provides the official reporting context for measures that include chronic absenteeism, College/Career Indicator, graduation, and suspension. Decision Lab uses CDE's official public data files as baseline inputs; it does not treat Dashboard reporting as a Decision Lab prediction.

OFFICIAL CALIFORNIA DATA INPUTS

The campus baseline is assembled from specific CDE public files—not from a generic statewide average.

Public Schools & DistrictsSchool identity, district, county and CDS code.
Census Day EnrollmentGrades 9–12 enrollment and campus population base.
Attendance & Chronic AbsenceChronic absence, students with absences and absence-day measures.
College/Career IndicatorPrepared, Approaching Prepared and related readiness measures.

Official marks and system names are shown for source identification only. Decision Lab is not a product of, or endorsed by, CDE, IES or NCES.
What this means for an administrator

Official data tells Decision Lab where your school is. Research helps describe the relationships underneath those outcomes. Decision Lab then models what could happen if you change goals, interventions, reach, overlap or staff constraints.

ADA Value · Per School

What These Two ADA Values Mean

The two numbers answer two different questions. Year 1 shows the immediate annual value of the modeled attendance recovery plus the first cohort of reconnected learners. Steady state shows what the annual value can look like once two returning reconnection cohorts overlap.

New ADA Value — Year 1
$0

Attendance Recovery + First-Year Reconnection Value.

Steady-State Annual ADA Value — Year 2+
$0

Attendance Recovery + two overlapping reconnection cohorts.

Why reconnection grows at steady state

The typical modeled reconnected learner returns around the beginning of junior year and remains enrolled for about two years. In Year 2, the prior year's returning cohort is still enrolled when the next cohort returns. Once that pattern repeats, the school carries approximately two overlapping reconnection cohorts in a normal year.

Year 1: annual attendance-recovery value + one year's new reconnection cohort.
Steady state: annual attendance-recovery value + two overlapping reconnection cohorts.
Attendance is not doubled: recovered attendance days are already an annual flow; only the retained reconnection population accumulates across cohorts.
These are modeled planning values, not guaranteed revenue. The current demonstration assumes an average of two years of retained enrollment for reconnected learners. A production model can replace that assumption with district-specific retention and enrollment-timing data.

How to read this page: Chronic Absence, CCI Prepared, Engaged, Reconnected Learners, and ADA Value reflect each school's latest completed RUN MODEL. Schools that have not been run are shown as Not Modeled and are excluded from district modeled-value totals. Clear removes only the saved summary result; the school returns automatically after its next completed run.

Year 1 vs. Steady State: Year 1 ADA Value combines the first year of modeled attendance recovery with the first cohort of reconnected students. Steady-State Annual ADA Value reflects the modeled annual value once reconnected students remain enrolled across overlapping school years. The current model assumes comparable new reconnection cohorts each year and approximately two years of retained enrollment. Attendance recovery is not doubled. Values are gross annualized planning estimates before costs.
